zones.label: Column 1
zones.note: Lexical checkpoint: Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, version 202510; supplied page subset consulted after independent scan reading. The scan remains authoritative. Source: https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html ; license: CC BY 4.0, https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ .

lines.note: Nos completes the preceding page's an-, in the definition of a term of years such as service. Nenki ga begins the next example; the repeated bottom nos, on f360 is therefore a catchword.

runs.text: Acabouſe a contia dos annos de ſer-

lines.note: Nenki ga hateta says that the agreed term has ended. The Portuguese translates the completion of a term of service and divides ſer-uiço across the next row.
Uiço completes ſeruiço, service, followed by the printed et cetera. This is body continuation, not page furniture.
Nenrai is many years or a long period, paraphrased by toshigoro. The abbreviated start Nẽ- of the example is entirely upright Japanese text.
Nenrai no nozomi means a wish held for many years. The Portuguese repeats that duration, closing the example begun above.
Nenrei means age, explained by toshi no yowai. The scan has two n types in Annos; the abbreviated relative q̃ leads into the next row.
The definition concerns the years each person has lived. Nenrei sakanna hito describes someone in the vigorous or youthful period of life.
The first example is translated as a young man. Nenrei yori mo fu- starts a contrasting example of appearing older than one's actual age.

runs.text: Esta mais velho do que tem de idade.

lines.note: Qeta completes fuketa, grown old. The Portuguese says the person is older-looking than the years of age would suggest.
Nenrio is reflection or foresight, explained by omoi and omonbakaru. Enlargement confirms a damaged ascender on b in vomonbacaru, not a nasal mark requiring contraction of the word.
Ção completes consideração, followed by providence or foresight. The upright S. marks written usage and is not part of the italic gloss.
Nenriki is the force of thought or concentration, paraphrased as omou chikara. The Portuguese penſamẽ- continues below.

The definition continues with thought or consideration, then starts the rock-penetrating proverb. The damaged con ideração is retained: consideration is plainly intended, but the missing long-s body is not recoverable enough to supply it as certain print.

runs.text: A força da imaginação, ou penſa-

lines.note: Touwosu completes the proverb that concentrated thought penetrates rock. The Portuguese translates the force of imagination or thought, continuing its last noun below.

runs.text: mento penetra rochas. i, pode muito.

lines.note: The proverb is explained as thought penetrating rocks, meaning that it is very powerful. This is the dictionary's figurative interpretation, not a literal claim by the reviewer.
Nenrǒ is an elderly person, paraphrased by toshiyori and glossed velho. Its caron differs from the circumflex in the anomalous New Year headword below.
Nensai denotes years or age. The two toshi words are printed separately, and the final S. is the upright written-register label.

runs.text: Figura, ou repreſentação de couſas que

lines.note: Nensǒ is a mental image or representation of imagined things. The short s and caron are retained as printed.
The relative clause completes things imagined. The upright Bup. labels the preceding definition as Buddhist terminology.

The gloss is the beginning of the year, semantically nentō. Enlargement nevertheless shows r in the printed Nenrô, repeated in the example below, so that apparent anomaly is preserved; Principio corrects the OCR's Princioio.
The New Year greeting repeats the printed Nenrôno rather than silently repairing it to Nentôno. Guioqei names the congratulatory occasion, followed by the Portuguese wish for good years.
Boas festas completes the New Year greeting as good festivities. It is a short Portuguese continuation of the preceding example.
Nenxi is another term for the beginning of the year, explained directly by toshi no hajime.

Nenxô is a child up to ten years old in this gloss. The alternative visibly ends in u, xôneu, although shōnen is intended; this apparent printed anomaly is retained rather than corrected from vocabulary alone. The final figure is 10, not OCR 1o.
Annos completes the age limit after 10 on the preceding row; the numeral and noun remain on their separate physical lines.
The damaged headword reads Nenxu, another beginning-of-year term. The surviving n before x corrects OCR Neuxu without changing the gloss.
Nenpǔ is a hot wind, paraphrased by atsuki kaze. The printed n before p and the caron over u are retained, and the final S. is a written-use label.
The principal forms of nerau are glossed as aiming or watching for an opportunity. The carons in ǒ and ǒta are retained rather than replaced with modern spellings.

runs.text: Apontar pera a tirar ao paſ

lines.note: Tori wo nerau is aiming to shoot a bird. The printed a tirar remains separated, and paſ continues into ſaro below without an invented line-end hyphen.
The first ſaro completes the bird word. Hito wo nerau then illustrates aiming at or lying in wait for a person; its purpose is specified on the next row.

runs.text: pera o matar, ou andar eſpreitando, & buſcã-

lines.note: The gloss specifies killing the person or watching for a chance. The scan supports matar with a, not OCR motar; buſcã- continues below.

runs.text: do enſejo pera matar a alguem. ¶

lines.note: The translation completes seeking an opportunity to kill. The next Japanese example begins Fumauo with m, not OCR Funauo; the following gloss identifies an opportunity or opening.
Nerǒ completes Fumauo nerǒ, seeking an opening or opportunity. The Portuguese enſejo supplies the sense of the Japanese expression.
The compound describes watching or stalking while moving around. The scan preserves a gap in Nera imauari and a visible initial N that OCR omitted.
This nere concerns a sword being bent or out of true. Torta is visibly printed, not the OCR's tarta; the example follows on the next row.
The sword example is followed by ki ga nereta, a bent piece of wood. The large initial Q was misrecognized as a second paragraph sign; one paragraph sign and Qiga are restored.
The piece of wood is crooked, completing the second example under this sense of nere.
The second nere means becoming thick, like batter or another substance cooked over a fire. It is distinct from the preceding crookedness entry.

runs.text: outrà couſa que ſe coze ao fogo. ¶

lines.note: The cooked-substance definition continues and then introduces silk as another subject. The printed outrà is retained rather than harmonized with modern outra.

runs.text: Eſtar a ſeda branda, & forte depo-

lines.note: Ito ga nereta describes silk becoming soft and strong after processing. The Portuguese depo- is completed by is on the following row.

runs.text: is de cozida, ou batida. ¶ Per met.

lines.note: After being cooked or beaten completes the silk-processing description. Per met. then introduces the figurative application to a person.
Nereta hito is a mature, settled person in this metaphorical use. The Portuguese assessment continues with peacefulness below.
Peaceful completes the description of the mature person; the short continuation belongs to the figurative example.
The transitive neru is thickening or making a substance dense. The scan reads Engroßar with o, not OCR Engrußar; al- continues into gũa.

runs.text: gũa couſa como polme, &c. ao fogo. ¶

lines.note: The substance is thickened over the fire like batter. The scan has a stop after &c., and Ito- begins the example about cooking or processing silk.
Ito wo neru means processing silk. Kane wo ne- begins a further example about working metal in a fire.

runs.text: Bater bem, & caldear no fogo fer

lines.note: Ri completes neri in neri kitǒ, working and forging metal. The Portuguese describes beating and heating it; fer continues into ro below without adding a conjectural hyphen.
Ro completes ferro, followed by metal and et cetera. The sentence closes the forging example at the bottom of the column.
This neri means walking very slowly. It begins a distinct verb sense, not a continuation of the metal-working example in column 1.
Foot before foot completes the image of slow, measured walking. The doubled vowels in pee are retained as historical spelling.
The noun Neri denotes a particular white Japanese alcoholic drink. The scan has r, correcting OCR Neti; the note does not impose a modern beverage classification.

runs.text: Calçoẽs feitos de certa laya de pe-

lines.note: Neribakama are trousers made from a certain kind of material. The Portuguese pe- continues into ça on the following row.
The material is white, completing the garment definition. This short row remains separate from the next bird headword.

runs.text: Calhandra no tempo que muda as

lines.note: Nerihibari is a lark during its change of feathers. The historical f in fibari is retained rather than modernized to h.

runs.text: penas que he no tempo do estio.

lines.note: The dictionary locates the feather change in summer. This is the source's seasonal description and completes the preceding bird entry.

runs.text: Figos de Iapão cozidos, ou tempe-

lines.note: Nerigaki are Japanese persimmons treated by cooking or steeping. Iapão begins with capital I, not OCR lowercase l; tempe- continues below.

runs.text: rados na agoa quente pera que não trauem. No

lines.note: The fruit is treated in hot water so it will not be astringent. No begins a regional comparison continued by Cami on the next row.
The term used in Cami is Auaxigaqi. Both are Japanese terms within a Portuguese regional explanation; they are flagged for whole-word typeface review, not treated as new headwords.
Neriguri is softened, cooked or processed silk. The gloss is complete on this line.
Neri ide is emerging or going out very slowly. The principal forms retain the printed separation and zz in zzuru; vagaroſa- continues below.
Mente completes vagarosamente, slowly. The line is part of the Portuguese adverb, not an independent dictionary item.
Nerinuki is a kind of silk fabric, clarified by kinu no tagui. The visible n before u corrects OCR Neriuuqi; the supplied NINJAL checkpoint agrees with the lexical identification.
Neriso denotes cooked or processed hemp threads. Canemo is retained in the Portuguese gloss rather than replaced by a modern technical term.
Nesosokurakashi describes preventing someone from sleeping. The principal forms and the repeated so sequence are retained, with the reason for the disturbance following below.

runs.text: mir a alguem zombando, ou fazendo traqui-

lines.note: The person is kept awake by joking or making a disturbance. The Portuguese traqui- is divided at the physical row boundary.
Nada completes traquinada, a commotion or prank, followed by et cetera. This closes the sleep-disturbing verb's definition.
Net means heat, explained by atsui and Portuguese quentura. The checked final t is not expanded to tçu in the transcription.
Netaba concerns a cutting edge, not a sewing thread; the following infinitive cortar establishes that sense of fio. The example begins netaba wo awasuru.

runs.text: Dar fio ſeco pera cortar derepen-

lines.note: Tsukuru is an alternative verb in the edge-making example. The Portuguese says to give it an edge for a sudden cut; derepen- continues below.
Te completes derepente, followed by quickly. The printed separation de preßa is preserved.

Netamagari means waking in fright; the worn central letters are read as amagari, supported by the residual g descender and the supplied NINJAL entry. The gloss's Epertar is retained without inventing an unestablished long s after E.
Fright completes the waking definition. The upright X. marks regional use; it is not italic continuation of the noun.
The verb netamu means envying or emulating. Its stem is Netami with a, not OCR Netimi; the caron and abbreviated principal forms are retained.
Netami is the corresponding noun, envy or emulation, as distinct from the preceding verb entry.
Netbiǒ is a febrile illness, paraphrased as an illness involving heat. The worn final-vowel mark is retained as the baseline caron; the sentence completes with febres below.
Fevers completes the Portuguese definition. This is an independent physical continuation line even though it contains only one word.

runs.text: Babas, que ſaem polla boca ao que eſtà

lines.note: Netçu denotes saliva issuing from the mouth during sleep. The following line completes the sleeping circumstance and supplies examples.
Netçu wo taruru or haku describes drooling while asleep. The alternatives and the attached object particle are retained in their printed forms.

runs.text: Babarſe dormindo: no cami ſe diz, Nezzu.

lines.note: The Portuguese explains drooling during sleep and gives Nezzu as the term in cami. The regional name and replacement term occur inside Portuguese prose and are flagged for typeface review.
Netçui and netçuifito describe a person who acts slowly and carefully. The printed closed compound netçuifito is retained rather than respaced from modern morphology.
Doing things slowly and exactly completes the person's characterization. The final sentence point is visible at the end of the row.
Netçuna has the same meaning, with the regional qualification printed closed as Noximo. Ximo is the regional name within this Portuguese explanation, not a new headword.
Netçuni and netçǔ are the adverbial counterparts of the preceding careful or slow quality. Aduer. supplies the grammatical label without a repeated full gloss.
Netoboke means being only half awake. The Portuguese meo is retained rather than modernized to meio.

runs.text: não dar acordo deſi de pois de eſpertar.

lines.note: The second paraphrase is not coming fully to one's senses after waking. The scan has continuous acordo, correcting OCR a cordo; the printed deſi and de pois remain unchanged.

runs.text: Paſſaro que eſtà pouſado nalgum lu-

lines.note: This netori is a bird perched to sleep. Paſſaro and pouſado restore the visibly present vowel and d lost in OCR; the grave in eſtà is retained from the scan.
Gar completes lugar, a place where the bird settles to sleep. The next netori is a different sense.

runs.text: Certo modo de tãger a frauta de Iapão.

lines.note: This netori is a manner of playing a Japanese flute. The scan supports tãger and the historical frauta, not the OCR's iãger and fruta; the word is not modernized to flauta.
Nettet is iron heated or glowing throughout in the fire. The doubled consonant and final checked t are retained.
Nettǒ is intensely hot water or a hot-water bath. The headword's caron contrasts with the circumflex in the following expression of regret.
Nhos completes banhos, baths of boiling water. The historical dagoa remains closed as printed.

runs.text: Palaura com que hum moſtra arrepen-

lines.note: Nettô introduces an expression of regret. The initial is N, not OCR X, and the circumflex is retained independently of the preceding hot-water entry.

runs.text: derſe de ter dito, ou feito algũa couſa. Vt,

lines.note: The speaker regrets having said or done something. The printed tilde in algũa is retained without shifting it to the adjacent vowel.

runs.text: A que não ouuera de to-

lines.note: The first example expresses regret over having formed an attachment or acquaintance. The scan supports Nettô rather than OCR Natrô; the Portuguese to- continues into mar below.
Mar completes tomar amizade. A second example begins Nettô mǒxitçu-, expressing regret over having said something; it continues on f362, whose opening is anticipated by the separate catchword.

zones.label: Column 2 catchword
zones.note: Anticipates the opening rǒ. A of f362; the Japanese continuation and Portuguese gloss are not additional body text here.
